newsitem.title: GREECE: Cyprus vows to deploy anti-aircraft missiles.
newsitem.headline: Cyprus vows to deploy anti-aircraft missiles.

text.p: Visiting Cypriot President Glafcos Clerides said on Thursday his country was determined to deploy newly-purchased Russian anti-aircraft missiles which have sent tensions soaring in the Eastern Mediterranean.

"There is no question of whether the S-300 missiles will be deployed, the S-300s will be deployed when they are ready and in accordance with the agreement with the Russians," Clerides told reporters on arrival at Athens airport.
Greece and Cyprus, independent since 1960, signed a military cooperation pact in 1993 and have worked to coordinate military strategy, exercises and materiel.
Clerides' visit coincides with the conclusion of a diplomatic shuttle by U.S. envoy Carey Cavanaugh to the countries caught up in the Cyprus missile crisis -- Cyprus, Greece and Turkey.
Cavanaugh was sent after Cyprus announced this month it was buying the missiles from Russia, and Turkey's quick response it would strike if necessary to ensure they were never deployed.
Clerides will meet Prime Minister Costas Simitis during his stay to discuss the joint defence agreement and, diplomats said, the hornets' nest stirred up by the Russian missile deal.
"The common Athens-Nicosia line towards Turkey will be reaffirmed during the visit. Cyprus does not stand alone in this dispute," a government official told Reuters.
But Greece's European Union allies as well as Washington and Turkey have all sharply criticised the missile purchase and said it was a destabilising mistake.

Turkey, which invaded Cyprus in 1974 and controls a third of the island, has threatened to use force to halt deployment of the S-300s. Defence experts have said that if deployed the S-300s would compromise Turkey's air supreriority in the region.
Greece has tried to play down the crisis but has also said Cyprus has the right to buy defensive weapons if it wishes.
The stand-off over the S-300s set alarm bells ringing in Washington and among Athens' EU partners and raised the spectre of a conflict involving NATO members Greece and Turkey.
Cavanaugh ended his trip to the region in Ankara on Thursday saying a potential crisis had been averted after a promise by Clerides that the S-300s would not be installed for another 16 months.
"This visit has turned out to be a successful diplomatic mission in what the United States was concerned could have been a crisis atmosphere," he said in Ankara.
"What we have been able to do is assure that there is a substantial period of time in which this issue can be addressed," he said.
Turkey has discounted Cavanaugh's optimism, saying the 16 months is meaningless because the missiles were not due to be delivered from Russia until mid-1998 anyway.

Cyprus has been divided since 1974 when Turkey invaded in response to a Greek Cypriot coup engineered by a military junta then ruling Greece. Ankara maintains some 30,000 troops in a self-declared Turkish Cypriot state in the north.
